Wider definitions that include all food and drink sold for out-of-home consumption put annual industry revenues considerably higher, in the region of USD 33 billion — a gap worth understanding before quoting a figure, because the two numbers describe different things rather than contradicting each other.

South Africa is the most developed foodservice supply chain on the continent, with established distributors, cash & carry operators and modern retail groups that buy for both retail and the professional channel, which makes it a realistic first African market for a supplier that has not exported to the region before. This study sets out market size and structure under each definition, profiles the distributors and importers that serve professional kitchens, explains the access requirements, documentation and import formalities for foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of South African importers and foodservice distribution partners.

metaDescription: USD 120–140bn, concentrated in the Seoul Capital Area. Market structure, access rules and a directory of Korean importers.
introduction:
South Korea offers roughly 51 million affluent, urban and digitally engaged consumers, concentrated heavily in the Seoul Capital Area. Estimates place the foodservice market at USD 120–140 billion in 2025, roughly KRW 150–190 trillion; several widely cited market-research houses put 2025 at about USD 126–138 billion and project continued strong growth, while USDA and ATO figures size the Hotel-Restaurant-Institutional sector at about KRW 140 trillion, around USD 122 billion.

The concentration of demand in one metropolitan region changes the entry calculation: national coverage is less important than the right partner in the capital area, and trends move quickly enough that a product's timing matters as much as its specification. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the distributors, cash & carry operators and specialist importers that serve the channel, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Korean importers and foodservice distributors.

metaDescription: Around EUR 130bn a year, distributed through two channels. Market structure, access requirements and a directory of importers.
introduction:
Spain's commercial foodservice sector turns over on the order of EUR 130 billion a year according to 2025 estimates, after a sharp recovery in recent years. It is one of the largest hospitality markets in Europe relative to its population, sustained by both domestic consumption and tourism, and with an establishment density far above the European average.

Distribution is led by a handful of national operators and is organised along two routes. On one side cash & carry — Makro, GM Cash and Gros Mercat — where the hospitality operator buys on a self-service basis; on the other, full-range delivered distributors such as Bidfood, Pro a Pro, DDI and Qualianza. For a foreign supplier, entry is decided by getting listed with one of them, not by direct selling to the restaurant. This study covers market volume and structure, the leading operators, access requirements by supplier origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Spanish importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.

metaDescription: SEK 163bn, with alcohol routed outside the retail monopoly. Market structure, access rules and a directory of Swedish importers.
introduction:
The Swedish out-of-home profit sector — restaurants, hotels, cafés, bars, catering and travel — generated revenue of approximately SEK 163 billion (around USD 15 billion) in 2023. Two demand patterns matter for a new supplier. Kitchen labour is scarce and costly, which puts pre-prepared and portioned formats in structural demand; and retail alcohol is sold only through the state monopoly Systembolaget, so the on-trade is supplied separately by importers and distributors to licence-holding venues — a distinction that changes the route to market for any beverage supplier.

A foreign supplier can enter through four partner types, and choosing the right one determines who to contact and what they will expect. Broadline foodservice wholesalers carry thousands of food and non-food lines and deliver nationwide, which suits products that can achieve volume across many outlets. Cash & carry operators are a fast route to trial and to independent restaurants and cafés. Retail groups with wholesale and import arms buy for both retail and foodservice and run large private-label programmes. Brand importers and distributors specialise in bringing international brands and private label into Sweden. This study covers market size and structure, access requirements by supplier origin, and a directory of Swedish importers and foodservice distributors.

metaDescription: Around CHF 30bn out-of-home, supplied by a few major wholesalers. Market structure, access rules and a directory of Swiss importers.
introduction:
The Swiss out-of-home market is today estimated at around CHF 30 billion a year; GastroSuisse already reported about CHF 23.6 billion in 2017, and the figure has grown since. Independent analyses put the commercial foodservice market for 2024 at roughly USD 16 to 17 billion, with expected annual growth of around 5 to 8 percent. Purchasing power and price levels make Switzerland attractive to foreign suppliers — and demanding at the same time.

The route to the customer runs through a handful of strong wholesalers. Transgourmet/Prodega (Coop) is the clear market leader; Saviva (Migros), Aligro/CCA Angehrn, TopCC (Spar) and the Pistor cooperative make up the rest of the leading group. Coop and Migros together control around a quarter of foodservice supply. For a new supplier, market entry therefore hinges on being listed with one of these houses. The study sets out market volume and channel structure, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU and from third countries, and includes a directory of Swiss importers and foodservice wholesalers.

metaDescription: USD 35bn heading to USD 50–55bn within six years. Market structure, access requirements and a directory of Thai importers.
introduction:
Thailand is one of ASEAN's most attractive and accessible foodservice markets. The Hotel-Restaurant-Institutional sector is estimated at approximately USD 35 billion in 2025 and is widely forecast to reach USD 50–55 billion within five to six years, implying compound annual growth in the region of 7 to 8%.

Supply reaches professional kitchens through three routes, and choosing the right one is the entry decision. Cash-and-carry and self-collect wholesalers — Makro and Go Wholesale — straddle retail and HoReCa and are the workhorse supply source for independent operators and SMEs. Full-range consumer-goods distributors serve both modern-trade retail and foodservice. And large operator groups buy centrally, among them PTT with its café and forecourt foodservice including Café Amazon, alongside international franchisors. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles those channels, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Thai importers and foodservice distribution partners.

metaDescription: 11 million tourists a year shaping demand. Market structure, access requirements and a directory of Tunisian importers.
introduction:
Tunisia is a Mediterranean market of roughly 12 million residents whose foodservice demand is amplified by a large and recovering tourism sector. In 2024 the country recorded about 10.25 million tourist arrivals — its highest level since 2010 — generating tourism revenue of roughly TND 7.05 billion, about US$2.3 billion, equivalent to close to 9% of GDP and supporting on the order of 400,000 jobs. In 2025 arrivals surpassed 11 million.

The composition of that visitor base shapes the menu and therefore the supply opportunity: the leading source markets are Algeria with about 3.1 million arrivals, largely across the land border, followed by Libya (about 1.4 million), France (1.2 million), Germany (560,000), the United Kingdom (410,000) and Italy (380,000). A supplier from any of those origins is selling into a market where its products already have a resident audience for part of the year. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the importers, distributors and retail groups that serve the channel, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, and provides a directory of Tunisian importers and foodservice distribution partners.

metaDescription: From USD 14bn to USD 44bn depending on scope. Market structure, customs union rules and a directory of Turkish importers.
introduction:
Türkiye combines a young population of roughly 85 million, rapid urbanisation and a large, recovering inbound-tourism sector. Published estimates of the foodservice market vary more than in most countries and it is worth knowing why before quoting a number: they range from roughly USD 14–15 billion on a profit-sector basis (Mordor Intelligence) to about USD 23 billion (MarketLine, 2024) and up to some USD 44 billion on the widest definitions. The differences are about scope — which channels and which parts of the institutional sector are counted — rather than about disagreement on the market's direction.

For a foreign supplier the route runs through importer-distributors that handle customs, certification and national distribution; Bidfood Türkiye and g2m are leading examples of the professional foodservice tier. This study sets out market size and structure under each definition, profiles the players, explains the access requirements for suppliers from the EU, from non-EU Europe and from outside Europe — Türkiye's customs union with the EU matters here and is treated explicitly — identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Turkish importers and foodservice distributors.

metaDescription: USD 18.6–23.2bn and no pan-market cash & carry chain. Market structure, access requirements and a directory of UAE importers.
introduction:
Published estimates of the UAE foodservice market for 2025 cluster between roughly USD 18.6 billion and USD 23.2 billion, with 2026 estimates around USD 27 billion and forecasts reaching USD 50–68 billion by 2033–2034 at double-digit compound growth. Mordor Intelligence, IMARC, Research & Markets, Renub Research and Market Data Forecast all publish figures in that band; the spread comes from scope rather than from any disagreement that this is one of the fastest-growing foodservice markets in the world.

Two structural features matter for a foreign supplier. The country imports the great majority of what its kitchens use, so imported supply is the norm rather than the exception. And there is no Metro or Makro-style pan-market cash-and-carry chain: the wholesale function sits with dedicated foodservice distributors, Bidfood Middle East (Horeca Trade LLC) being the largest in the country, alongside operators such as Admirals, Chef Middle East and Aramtec. This study covers market size and structure under each published definition, profiles those distributors, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of UAE importers and foodservice distributors.

metaDescription: £80–90bn out-of-home, reached through wholesalers rather than direct. Market structure, post-Brexit access rules and a directory of importers.
introduction:
The United Kingdom is one of the largest and most dynamic foodservice markets in Europe. Depending on scope and methodology, the total out-of-home market is valued at roughly US$100–111 billion (about £80–90 billion) across 2025–2026, and is forecast to keep growing at a mid-single-digit annual rate for the rest of the decade. For an exporter the attraction is not only the size of the market but its openness: a high share of imported food and drink, a settled appetite for world cuisines, and a highly organised wholesale layer that can give a new supplier national coverage through a single partner.

The decisive structural fact is that almost no foreign supplier sells directly to UK restaurants, pubs or hotels. The market is reached through wholesalers, cash-and-carry operators, buying groups and specialist importers, who act as the UK food business operator and importer of record, handle post-Brexit border formalities and warehousing, and own the sales relationship with the end operator. Choosing the right partner — by channel, product category and country of origin — is therefore the market-entry decision that matters. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles the major players, explains access requirements differentiated by supplier origin, identifies the product groups with the strongest prospects, and provides a working directory of UK importers and distribution partners.

metaDescription: High income, 3.4 million residents and tourism that broadens demand. Market structure, access rules and a directory of importers.
introduction:
Uruguay is a compact, high-income economy with about 3.4 million residents. Its distinguishing feature for a supplier lies in tourism: the country received around 3.6 million visitors — more than its own resident population — with revenue close to USD 2,040 million. The supermarket sector turns over on the order of USD 2,500 million a year, a useful reference for sizing demand for packaged food.

Final consumer spending on restaurants is estimated on the order of USD 1,500 to 2,500 million a year. The range is deliberately wide: for a market of this size the available sources offer orders of magnitude rather than precise figures, and this study flags that wherever it occurs. The document covers the structure of the market and its channels, access requirements by supplier origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Uruguayan importers and distributors in the HORECA channel.

metaDescription: Roughly USD 1,080 million in 2025, projected to reach USD 1,900 by 2032. Structure, channel access and importer directory.
introduction:
Venezuela's food and beverage market was estimated at around USD 1,080 million in 2025, with projections pointing to some USD 1,900 million by 2032, at a high single-digit compound growth rate. It is a small market by value and an atypical one in how it works: the de facto dollarisation of a large part of transactions has substantially changed purchasing conditions compared with the previous decade.

For a foreign supplier, that means the older market references describe a country that no longer exists commercially, and that the choice of importer — for its access to foreign currency, its logistics and its customer base — matters more than in any other market in the region. This study sets out the structure of the market and its channels, the access and import requirements according to the supplier's origin and the categories with the best prospects, and includes a directory of Venezuelan importers and distributors in the HoReCa channel.

metaDescription: USD 24–25bn growing at 9–11% a year. Market structure, access requirements and a directory of Vietnamese importers.
introduction:
Vietnam's foodservice market is estimated at roughly USD 24–25 billion in 2025 and is widely forecast to grow at a compound annual rate of about 9 to 11%, putting it on a path toward USD 41–54 billion within the next five to nine years. Growth is powered by a young and urbanising population, more than 18 million international arrivals, and the accelerating digitalisation of ordering and payment.

For a foreign supplier, Vietnam is at the stage where imported specialty and branded products are moving from the top-end hotel segment into the wider commercial restaurant base — which is the window in which an entrant can establish a position before the category is crowded. The route runs through licensed importers and distributors that handle registration, customs and cold chain. This study sets out market size and structure, profiles those partners, explains the access requirements and documentation for foreign suppliers, identifies the categories with the strongest prospects, and provides a directory of Vietnamese importers and foodservice distribution partners.

metaDescription: Premium em vez de volume e certificação como ingresso de entrada. Situação do mercado, requisitos e diretório de importadores alemães.
introduction:
A Alemanha é um dos maiores e mais ricos mercados consumidores de fruta fresca da Europa e, por não ter produção tropical própria, depende quase inteiramente de importação. Para produtores da África, da América Central e da América do Sul isso torna o mercado estruturalmente atraente — e, ao mesmo tempo, muito disputado e exigente. As oportunidades não estão no negócio de massa de banana e abacaxi, de margem baixa, mas no segmento premium e de especialidades — sobretudo abacate, frutas vermelhas, manga e maracujá — e nos nichos orgânico e Fairtrade.

A certificação é, na prática, o ingresso de entrada: do lado legal, o certificado fitossanitário e o cumprimento dos limites máximos de resíduos; do lado comercial, GLOBALG.A.P. e GRASP e, sobre eles, orgânico e/ou Fairtrade ou Rainforest Alliance. Para quem está começando, o caminho passa quase sempre por um importador estabelecido: fornecer diretamente às centrais de compra do varejo alemão — EDEKA Fruchtkontor, REWE Eurogroup — só se torna realista com volume, certificação completa e histórico comprovado. O fator decisivo é escolher importadores que de fato aceitam novos produtores, e a lista de contatos deste estudo é filtrada e classificada segundo esse critério.

metaDescription: Premium antes que volumen y certificación como billete de entrada. Situación del mercado, requisitos y directorio de importadores.
introduction:
Alemania es uno de los mercados de fruta fresca más grandes y con mayor poder adquisitivo de Europa y, al carecer de producción tropical propia, depende casi por completo de la importación. Para los productores de África, Centroamérica y Sudamérica esto convierte al mercado en estructuralmente atractivo y, a la vez, muy competido y exigente. Las oportunidades no están en el negocio masivo de banano y piña, de margen bajo, sino en el segmento premium y de especialidades —sobre todo aguacate, frutos rojos, mango y maracuyá— y en los nichos ecológico y de comercio justo.

La certificación es en la práctica el billete de entrada: en lo legal, el certificado fitosanitario y el cumplimiento de los límites máximos de residuos; en lo comercial, GLOBALG.A.P. y GRASP y, sobre ellos, ecológico y/o Fairtrade o Rainforest Alliance. Para quien empieza, el camino pasa casi siempre por un importador establecido: suministrar directamente a las centrales de compra del comercio alemán —EDEKA Fruchtkontor, REWE Eurogroup— solo resulta realista con volumen, certificación completa y trayectoria demostrable. El factor decisivo es elegir importadores que realmente incorporen nuevos productores, y el listado de contactos de este estudio está filtrado y valorado con ese criterio.

metaDescription: Europe's largest market for plant-based alternatives. Channel structure, access requirements and a directory of importers.
introduction:
Germany is Europe's largest market for plant-based alternatives and one of the most mature worldwide: meat, dairy and cheese alternatives have long since arrived on the mainstream shelf, the share of own-label products is rising and price pressure is increasing, while growth shifts from the niche into broad retail and foodservice. For a foreign manufacturer, what counts is therefore less the innovation lead than the ability to meet listing, logistics and labelling requirements in German retail.

This study sets out the market volume and channel structure for plant-based alternatives, names the leading retail and foodservice players, describes the access requirements and labelling rules for suppliers from the EU and from third countries, and includes a directory of German importers and distributors.

metaDescription: 11.8 million inhabitants and heavy reliance on imports. Market, labelling requirements and a directory of Belgian toy importers.
introduction:
Belgium is a small, wealthy and densely populated market of around 11.8 million inhabitants, located between three of Europe's largest markets. Its commercial particularity is first and foremost linguistic: the country has three official languages — Dutch, spoken by around 60% of the population in Flanders, French, around 40% in Wallonia and predominantly in Brussels, and German for a small community in the east. For a toy supplier, this shapes labelling, packaging and documentation from the very first order.

It is also a logistics hub heavily dependent on imports, with China alone supplying nearly half the imported value. A gap has opened recently: the average retail price has reached a record level while the average import price has fallen appreciably. The directory in chapter 8 lists Belgian importers, distributors, importing retailers and non-food wholesalers, distinguishing toy specialists from importers for whom toys are just one non-food category among many, and separating full-range importers, range specialists, institutional suppliers and large chains that import on their own account.

metaDescription: EUR 4.7bn in 2025, up 7.1% — the best year since 2000. Leading categories, access conditions and a directory of French importers.
introduction:
The French toy and games market reached around EUR 4.7 billion in 2025, up 7.1% in value and 7% in volume according to Circana — the strongest annual growth recorded in France since 2000, ahead of the United Kingdom (+6.1%) and Germany (+3.2%). A commercially important fact: this growth did not come from prices. The average price remained stable, at around EUR 18 over the year and EUR 21 during the Christmas period. Volumes, therefore, are what grew.

The momentum is concentrated in a few categories: strategic collectible cards (around +78%, led by Pokémon), construction (+32 to +35%, driven by LEGO), audio story players (+63%), card games (+16%) and traditional plush (+11%). Collecting, across categories, grew by around 45% and now accounts for nearly 13% of market value, while licences weigh around 30%. Distribution remains concentrated without being closed, with the toy specialist accounting for 37 to 44% of sales. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners established outside France and includes a directory of French toy importers and distributors.

metaDescription: EUR 4.4bn in sales with retail in few hands. Market figures, safety rules and a directory of leading German toy importers.
introduction:
Germany is the largest single toy market in continental Europe. Sales at end-consumer prices across all distribution channels came to around EUR 4.4 billion in 2024, and the German toy trade association (BVS), together with Circana, expected growth of about three percent for 2025. The market is attractive precisely because it is demanding: product safety rules are strict and are being tightened further, and retail buying is concentrated in comparatively few hands.

Between a good product and shelf space in Germany there is, as a rule, an importer or distributor, not the retailer itself. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners outside Germany that already sell successfully in their home market and now want to enter under their own brand or as a private-label supplier. It covers traditional toys, games and puzzles, trading cards, video games as an adjacent category, and playground, nursery and school equipment. At its core is a directory of German importers, distributors, buying associations and direct-importing retailers, which deliberately distinguishes toy specialists from more broadly based non-food importers — the two negotiate differently and expect different things from a new supplier.

metaDescription: EUR 1.8 to 2.5 billion at retail, with a strong weight of large-scale retail. Market, requirements and a list of Italian importers.
introduction:
The Italian market for traditional toys, excluding video games, is worth in the order of EUR 1.8–2.5 billion at retail depending on the measurement scope, while the video games market alone exceeds EUR 2 billion. Broadening the view to total spending on children and Gen Z — including clothing, publishing and licensed products — the estimated value exceeds EUR 7 billion.

Distribution does not run only through specialist shops. Large-scale retail chains — Esselunga, Coop, Conad, Selex — and non-food discounters absorb significant seasonal volumes and buy a great deal under private label, which opens a concrete door to a foreign supplier still without brand awareness in Italy. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners based outside Italy, covers market size, channel structure and the technical and regulatory requirements for placing toys on the Italian market, and includes a list of importers, distributors and retailers that import on their own account.

metaDescription: Around EUR 1.4 billion and growth of 6 to 7% a year. Market size, legal requirements and an overview of Dutch toy importers.
introduction:
The Netherlands has around 18 million inhabitants with high household purchasing power, virtually full internet penetration and compact geography — a combination that makes nationwide distribution through a single partner realistic. The market for toys and games was valued at around USD 1.5 billion in 2025, equivalent to roughly EUR 1.4 billion, with expected growth to some USD 2.7 billion by the mid-2030s — annual growth of about 6 to 7%.

Within that market, the board games and puzzles segment is among the fastest growing, worth around USD 0.22 billion in 2025. For a foreign manufacturer or brand owner, the route to the shelf in the Netherlands almost always runs through an importer or distributor and not through the retailer itself. This study is written for suppliers of both branded products and private label, covers market size, channel structure and the legal and technical requirements for placing toys on the Dutch market, and includes an overview of Dutch importers, distributors and direct-importing retailers.

metaDescription: One of the smallest in Western Europe, but stable. Size, legal requirements and a directory of importers and distributors.
introduction:
Portugal is one of the smallest toy markets in Western Europe, but stable. With a population of around 10.5 million, the toy and games market stands, at retail value, at around EUR 300 to 400 million a year. The range should be read as indicative: available sources measure on different bases — import value, retail value or a single subcategory — and published figures diverge considerably.

The supply structure depends heavily on imports, and Spain is by far the main supplier: around USD 141 million in dolls and toys, approximately 47% of the total imported. Marketplaces and online retailers, with Amazon.es serving the Portuguese market, are the fastest-growing channel. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners based outside Portugal, discusses the size and structure of the market and the legal and technical requirements for placing toys on the Portuguese market, and includes a directory of importers, distributors and retailers that import on their own account.

metaDescription: Between EUR 1,200 and 1,500 million, Europe's fourth or fifth largest. Market, legal requirements and a directory of Spanish importers.
introduction:
The Spanish market for traditional toys stands in a range of EUR 1,200 to 1,400 million in retail sales in recent years, and reaches EUR 1,500 million or more depending on the source and on whether video games and baby care items are included. Spain is Europe's fourth or fifth largest market by size, and published figures vary appreciably because each data provider measures on a different scope.

Distribution combines vertical toy chains with generalist large-format stores — Carrefour, Alcampo/Auchan — which buy relevant volumes of own brand and private label, a realistic entry route for a foreign manufacturer still without brand awareness in Spain. Between the product and the shelf there is almost always a Spanish importer or distributor, not the retailer directly. This study is aimed at manufacturers and brand owners established outside Spain, discusses the size and structure of the market and the legal and technical requirements for marketing toys, and includes a directory of importers, distributors and retailers that import on their own account.

metaDescription: £3.9bn at retail, with adults now 31% of spend. Market size, safety requirements and a directory of UK toy importers and distributors.
introduction:
The United Kingdom is one of Europe's largest toy markets. The British Toy & Hobby Association and most of the trade value it at approximately £3.9 billion at retail; on Circana's European comparison the UK sits just over €5 billion, ahead of both France and Germany. Published figures differ widely because providers measure on different bases — retail against trade value, and varying treatment of trading cards, video games and licensed non-toy merchandise — which is why this study names the source behind every figure it quotes.

Two structural features shape the opening for a newcomer. Adult buyers are now the single largest segment: toys bought by and for people aged 12 and over grew about 5% in the twelve months to June 2025 and are worth roughly £1.2 billion, some 31% of total toy spend, or about £1 in every £3, with 43% of adults aged 18 and over buying toys for themselves. Preschool remains the volume engine at roughly 17% of spend and 22% of units, at an average purchase price near £8.54. This study is written for manufacturers and brand owners based outside the UK, whether branded or private-label, and its core is a directory of UK importers, distributors and direct-importing retailers that separates dedicated toy specialists from general non-food importers carrying toys as one category among many.
